title: Linked List Cycle II
description: Brute force to optimized: a visited-node set versus the two-phase Floyd's algorithm that locates the exact cycle-start node in O(1) space.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given the head of a linked list, return the node where the cycle begins, if the linked list has a cycle. If there is no cycle, return null.

blocks.caption: Slow/fast pointers detect a cycle; a second phase then locates exactly where it begins

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
This builds directly on detecting whether a cycle exists (Linked List Cycle), but now the exact node where the cycle begins must be identified and returned, not just a true/false answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Where a Running Track's Loop Begins
blocks.text: Two runners, one twice as fast as the other, start at the same point on a track that has a straight starting stretch leading into a circular loop. If they ever meet again, it proves the loop exists. Surprisingly, if one runner then goes back to the very start and both continue at the SAME (slow) pace, they will meet again exactly at the point where the loop begins. This is not a coincidence, it follows directly from the distances involved.

blocks.caption: After the first meeting point, resetting one pointer to the head and moving both at equal speed lands exactly on the cycle's start

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: head = [3,2,0,-4], the tail (-4) connects back to index 1 (value 2)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Slow/fast pointers eventually meet somewhere inside the cycle","A cycle is confirmed to exist","A faster pointer confined to a loop must eventually catch up to a slower one"],["A third pointer starts at head; it and slow both advance 1 step at a time until they meet","They meet at the node valued 2 (index 1)","This is exactly the cycle's starting node"],["Answer","The node valued 2","Matches the known cycle entry point"]]}

blocks.text: Example: head = [1], no cycle (pos = -1)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["fast reaches the end of the list (null) without ever meeting slow","No cycle exists","fast.next becomes null, ending the search"],["Answer","null","There is no cycle to locate"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before reaching for a hash set of visited nodes, notice that the classic slow/fast pointer technique used to DETECT a cycle can be extended with one extra phase to also LOCATE where it begins, using no extra memory.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Using slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps) pointers, if a cycle exists, they are guaranteed to meet somewhere inside it, exactly as in the plain cycle-detection problem.

Observation 2: Let the distance from the head to the cycle's start be "a", and the distance from the cycle's start to the meeting point be "b". By the time they meet, fast has traveled exactly twice the distance slow has.

Observation 3: Working through the distance equations (a well-known derivation), it turns out that the remaining distance from the meeting point back around to the cycle's start is exactly equal to "a", the distance from the ORIGINAL head to the cycle's start.

Observation 4: This means: reset one pointer to the head, keep the other at the meeting point, and advance BOTH one step at a time. They are mathematically guaranteed to meet again exactly at the cycle's starting node.

Recognizing this second phase (reset-and-walk-together) turns a simple yes/no cycle detector into a full cycle-locator, still using only O(1) extra space.
This is Floyd's cycle detection algorithm extended with a second phase that exploits a precise distance relationship between the meeting point and the cycle's actual start.
6. Brute Force Solution
Walk the list one node at a time, remembering every node visited. The first node seen for a SECOND time is exactly where the cycle begins.
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk the list, adding each node to a visited set as it is reached.
The moment a node is encountered that is ALREADY in the visited set, that node is the cycle's starting point; if the list ends (null) first, there is no cycle.

codes.python:
def detect_cycle(head):
    visited = set()
    node = head
    while node:
        if id(node) in visited:                                            # a node seen twice means this is where the cycle begins
            return node
        visited.add(id(node))
        node = node.next
    return None                                                             # reached the end with no repeats: no cycle


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(3, ListNode(2, ListNode(0, ListNode(-4))))
    head.next.next.next.next = head.next
    result = detect_cycle(head)
    print(result.val if result else "None")

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A set of visited node references (identity, not value) is used, since two different nodes could coincidentally share the same value.

The very first repeated node encountered must be the cycle's start, since every node strictly before the cycle is visited exactly once, and the cycle's start is the first node reachable a second time.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This correctly identifies the cycle's start (or confirms no cycle exists) by definition, since it directly tracks every node ever visited.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass through the list.
Space: O(n), for the set of visited node references.
Limitation: the O(n) extra space for tracking every visited node is unnecessary; a two-phase two-pointer approach solves the exact same problem using only O(1) extra space.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force needs O(n) space just to remember which nodes have been seen. Instead, run the standard slow/fast pointer race until they meet (confirming a cycle exists). Then, reset ONE pointer back to the head, and advance both remaining pointers at the SAME speed (1 step each). The mathematically guaranteed meeting point of this second phase is exactly the cycle's starting node.

Phase 1: advance slow by 1 and fast by 2 until they meet, or fast reaches the end (no cycle, return null). Phase 2: reset a pointer to head; advance it and slow together, 1 step at a time, until they meet; that meeting point is the cycle's start.
9. Optimized Solution
Use the two-phase slow/fast pointer technique: detect the cycle first, then locate its start with a second, equal-speed walk.
Dry run for head = [3,2,0,-4], tail connects back to index 1 (value 2)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Both pointers meet at the node valued 2 (index 1), confirming it as the cycle's starting node, matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def detect_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:                                                    # slow and fast met: a cycle exists somewhere
            ptr = head
            while ptr is not slow:                                          # both now move at the SAME speed (1 step)
                ptr = ptr.next
                slow = slow.next
            return ptr                                                      # they must meet exactly at the cycle's start
    return None                                                             # fast reached the end: no cycle


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(3, ListNode(2, ListNode(0, ListNode(-4))))
    head.next.next.next.next = head.next
    result = detect_cycle(head)
    print(result.val if result else "None")

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), both phases together still visit each node a bounded number of times.
Space: O(1) extra, only a few pointers are used.
Why This Works

Let "a" be the distance from head to the cycle's start, "b" the distance from the cycle's start to the meeting point, and "c" the remaining distance around the cycle back to the start. When slow and fast first meet, slow has traveled (a + b), and fast has traveled (a + b + c + b), which is exactly double slow's distance. Solving that equation shows a = c (the distance from the ORIGINAL head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point onward back to the start). That is precisely why resetting one pointer to the head and advancing both remaining pointers at equal speed causes them to meet exactly at the cycle's start.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Phase 1: fast reaches null","No cycle exists; return null immediately"],["Phase 1: slow and fast meet","A cycle exists; proceed to phase 2 to locate its start"],["Phase 2: pointer from head and slow meet","This meeting point is exactly the cycle's starting node"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Phase 1 is identical to the plain Linked List Cycle detection: slow advances 1 step, fast advances 2, checked for a meeting after each step.
Phase 2 only begins once a meeting is confirmed; it resets exactly one of the two pointers to head, keeping the other at the meeting point.
Both pointers in phase 2 move at the SAME speed (1 step), which is what makes the distance relationship (a = c) produce a guaranteed meeting at the cycle's start.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Floyd's cycle detection extends naturally into a second phase: once slow and fast meet, resetting one pointer to the head and advancing both at equal speed locates the exact cycle-start node, using no extra memory.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting that phase 2 must advance BOTH pointers at the SAME speed (1 step each), not continuing the 1-vs-2 speed ratio from phase 1.
Not handling the no-cycle case, where fast (or fast.next) becomes null before any meeting ever occurs.
Assuming the meeting point from phase 1 IS the cycle's start, without running the required second phase.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Being able to derive (or at least clearly explain) WHY the phase-2 reset works, using the a = c distance relationship, demonstrates a much deeper understanding than simply memorizing the two-phase steps.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find WHERE a cycle begins" (not just whether one exists) points toward extending Floyd's slow/fast detection with a second, equal-speed phase starting from the head.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also determine the LENGTH of the cycle? Once slow and fast meet, keep one pointer fixed and advance the other until it returns to the same node, counting the steps taken.

Can you prove the a = c distance relationship rather than just stating it? Walk through the algebra: fast's distance (a + b + c + b) equals 2 times slow's distance (a + b), which simplifies directly to a = c.
How does this compare to the plain Linked List Cycle (detection only) problem? This is a direct two-phase extension of that same slow/fast pointer foundation.

items: A direct two-phase extension of the plain Linked List Cycle detection problem elsewhere in this category, reusing its exact slow/fast pointer foundation.

Optimized (two-phase Floyd's algorithm): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Two-phase Floyd's cycle detection (detect, then locate the start)
Core Idea: After slow and fast meet, resetting one pointer to head and advancing both at equal speed meets exactly at the cycle's start, due to a proven distance relationship
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: The distance from the original head to the cycle's start always equals the remaining distance from the meeting point back around to that same start
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Meet once (detect), reset one pointer to head, meet again at equal speed (locate)
